lesson.subject: literacy
lesson.title: Open Strong
lesson.subtitle: Term 4 Week 4, Session 2
lesson.footer: Persuasive Writing | Year 5/6 Literacy | Week 4 Session 2

plan.curriculum: English 2.0, Level 5: VC2E5LA03 how persuasive texts are organised into stages; VC2E5LA04 using the start of a paragraph to give prominence to the message; VC2E5LY10 creating texts with sequenced ideas for an audience
plan.shape: order, label, draft: students order a shuffled introduction, label the parts of a new one, then draft their own, because the four moves are quick to learn and the drafting time is what matters
plan.criticalFeature: by the end of the introduction the reader knows exactly what you want and why
decisionPoints: the choice check: what is missing?
the exit board: a missing preview written
plan.anchor: Claim it. Prove it. Sell it. The introduction sells first, then claims, then previews the proof.
plan.catchUp: Missed Session 1? Five-minute plan with the teacher: issue, reader, position, three reasons. Then use the Introduction Frame.

studentTools: Writing books (draft on every second line)
routineIcons: Write it, chin it, show me
Point to A, B or C
boardSetup: The four parts of an introduction: 1 hook, 2 context, 3 position, 4 preview
Drafting rule on the board: skip a line, so there is room to revise in Week 5

resources.label: Worksheet
resources.description: Your turn: label the parts, find what's missing, write previews, then plan your own introduction.
resources.title: Open Strong
resources.subtitle: Hook, context, position, preview.

example.prompt: 'Right now, our pool closes at 4 pm.'
steps: Does it explain what's happening? Context

items.prompt: Label each sentence: hook, context, position or preview.
rows: Our pool should stay open until 7 pm.
What if summer evenings were spent splashing, not scrolling?
Longer hours mean fitter kids, safer swimming and happier families.
Right now, the pool shuts at 4 pm, just as school ends.
Imagine a 35-degree evening with nowhere to cool off.
answers: Our pool should stay open until 7 pm.
What if summer evenings were spent splashing, not scrolling?
Longer hours mean fitter kids, safer swimming and happier families.
Right now, the pool shuts at 4 pm, just as school ends.
Imagine a 35-degree evening with nowhere to cool off.

items.prompt: 'Have you ever tripped on our broken path? It has been cracked for two years. The council must fix it.' What's missing?
items.explain: There is no preview of the reasons coming.

items.prompt: Ella's preview is too long. Find the problem and fix it.
work: Gardens give food, shade, science, calm, birds, bees, jobs and fun.
items.answer: Eight reasons is a list, not a preview. Fix: A garden feeds our canteen, teaches science and calms busy minds.

example.prompt: Position: we need more bins. Reasons: less litter, fewer pests, a cleaner oval.
steps: Cut each reason to a few words
example.answer: More bins mean less litter, fewer pests and, most importantly, a cleaner oval.

items.prompt: Write a one-line preview for each position.
rows: Ban phones at lunch: play, friendships, rest for eyes
Start school later: sleep, focus, safer mornings
Plant more trees: shade, birds, cooler rooms
answers: Ban phones at lunch: play, friendships, rest for eyes
Phone-free lunches mean more play, real friendships and rested eyes.
Start school later: sleep, focus, safer mornings
A later start means more sleep, sharper focus and safer mornings.
Plant more trees: shade, birds, cooler rooms
Trees bring shade, birds and, most importantly, cooler classrooms.

steps: Position and preview from your plan
example.answer: Hook: Imagine twenty steps... Position: stop bringing in new bears.

items.prompt: Plan your four parts in a few words each. Then draft it in your writing book, every second line.
answers: one or two sentences: what's happening

resources.label: Extension
resources.description: Early finisher option: link the four parts smoothly, then write the opening for a second reader.
resources.title: Opening Moves
resources.subtitle: Great introductions flow.

example.prompt: Hook: Imagine twenty steps. Context: In the wild, bears roam hundreds of kilometres.
steps: Add a linking word or phrase
example.answer: Imagine twenty steps a day. Yet in the wild, a bear roams hundreds of kilometres.

items.prompt: Join each pair so they flow. Use a linking word or phrase.
answers: What if lunch were longer? Right now, it lasts only 40 minutes.
Imagine a shady playground. Sadly, ours has just two small trees.
Have you seen our river? Every day, rubbish floats past.

example.answer: Year 3: Polar bears need lots of room. Zoos are too small.

items.prompt: Write your introduction again for a Year 3 class. Keep all four parts.
items.answer: Four parts in short, simple sentences.

resources.label: Supported Worksheet
resources.description: Supported option: picture-clue choices, starters for each part and a frame.
resources.title: Introduction Helper
resources.subtitle: Four parts: hook, context, position, preview.

steps: Does it say what should happen?

items.prompt: Imagine a beach with no rubbish.
Have you ever been too hot?
items.hint: A question to pull you in.

steps: Position: I am writing to ask...
example.answer: Imagine twenty steps. Right now, bears live in small zoos. I am writing to ask you to stop.

items.prompt: Finish each starter for your issue.
rows: I am writing to ask you to ...
answers: I am writing to ask you to ...
items.hint: Write your words after each starter.

items.prompt: Copy your best sentence from your introduction. Which part is it?

slides.notes: Open the session. One line: today you write the first paragraph your reader will ever see.

Print the Worksheet for everyone, the Extension for early finishers and the Supported Worksheet for those who need it. Students need their big piece plan from Session 1. Drafts go in writing books, every second line.

slides.learningIntention: We are learning to write an introduction that tells the reader exactly where we stand.
successCriteria: I can name the four parts of an introduction.
I can write an introduction with a hook, context, position and preview.
I can make my introduction fit my reader so they keep reading.

beats: POINT to the learning intention.
SAY: Your reader decides in one paragraph whether to take you seriously.
SAY: Read the I can lines with me. Everyone, together, on three.
SAY: Naming the four parts is where we start.
Writing all four for your issue is today's main goal.
notes.prep: SC1 naming the parts is reachable for all; SC2 writing all four is the core and the exit evidence; SC3 fitting the reader is the stretch.

slides.title: Put it back together
lines: A: I am writing to ask you to stop bringing in new polar bears.
B: Imagine walking the same twenty steps, every day, for thirty years.
C: They need space, they are built for cold, and the money could help wild bears.
D: In the wild, a polar bear can roam hundreds of kilometres.

notes.answer: B, D, A, C - hook, context, position, preview
beats: SAY: Four sentences from one introduction. They're jumbled.
Which one should come first?
ASK: Which sentence starts it?
5 sec. Cue: voices off, everyone points to A, B, C or D.
EXPECT: pointing to B
ASK: What's the whole order? Tell your partner.
20 sec. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: B, D, A, C
SAY: Hook, what's happening, what I want, what's coming. Today you write yours.
trap: putting the position first because it's most important.
Fix: ask would the reader keep going? Student moves the hook up.
notes.prep: Mixed-start ordering task (megaprompt 19a); the correct order is only in these notes. Retrieves Week 3 hooks. 3 minutes.

slides.meaning: A sneak peek at the reasons that are coming.
slides.example: They need space, they are built for cold, and the money could help wild bears.

notes.answer: a sneak peek at the reasons that are coming
beats: POINT to the word. SAY: Preview. Say it with me. Preview.
SAY: Like a movie trailer. It shows what's coming without the whole story.
One short line naming your three reasons.
ASK: How many reasons does the example preview?
5 sec. Cue: Fingers at your chest... show me.
EXPECT: 3
trap: writing the whole of each reason in the preview.
Fix: student cuts each reason to a few words.
notes.prep: The part students most often leave out. The trailer image carries it.

slides.title: Watch me open strong
slides.extract: Dear Zoo Director, Imagine walking the same twenty steps, every day, for thirty years. In the wild, a polar bear can roam hundreds of kilometres in search of food. I am writing to ask you to stop bringing new polar bears into your zoo. Polar bears need far more space than any zoo can give, they are built for the cold, and the money could do much more good in the Arctic.
highlights: Imagine walking the same twenty steps
In the wild, a polar bear can roam
I am writing to ask you to stop
they are built for the cold
slides.source: Model letter, written for this session

beats: POINT to Imagine.
SAY: My hook from last week. It pulls the director in.
POINT to In the wild.
SAY: Context: what's happening. Now the director knows the problem.
POINT to I am writing to ask.
SAY: My position. Clear, polite, and it says exactly what I want.
ASK: Which part is my last sentence?
5 sec. Cue: Fingers at your chest, 1 hook, 2 context, 3 position, 4 preview... now.
EXPECT: 4, preview
trap: context that tells the whole story of the novel.
Fix: student keeps one or two sentences: just enough to see the problem.
notes.stretch: Make your preview's last reason the strongest.
notes.help: Introduction Frame: one starter per part.
notes.prep: The model, the same zoo letter used all week. Critical feature: by the end the reader knows exactly what you want and why.

slides.title: Which part?
slides.pivot: ask: does it pull, explain, claim or list?
slides.followUp: cold call one student: which words told you?

items.text: We should turn the empty land behind the library into a vegetable garden.
Have you ever eaten a tomato straight off the vine?
A garden would feed our canteen, teach science outdoors and calm busy minds.
Right now, that land is just weeds and broken pavers.

say: A new introduction, chopped up and mixed.
trap: calling the preview a position because it sounds certain.
Fix: ask is it a list of reasons? Then it's the preview.
notes.stretch: Say the correct order of all four.
notes.help: Look for a question first: that's often the hook.
notes.prep: Guided labelling on a new issue, in mixed order. SC1.

slides.title: What is missing from this introduction?
slides.prompt: Too hot to learn? Our rooms hit 30 degrees. We must have air conditioning.

options.misconception: misses that the question is the hook
misses that We must... is the position

notes.answer: C - there is no preview of the reasons
beats: SAY: Read it in your head. Count the parts.
ASK: What is missing from this introduction?
15 sec. Cue: voices off, everyone points to A, B or C.
EXPECT: pointing to C
SCAN the room, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, cold call: write the missing preview aloud.
Less -> label each sentence 1, 2, 3 together, re-ask.
REVEAL after pointing is scanned.
SAY: The preview. The reader doesn't know what reasons are coming.
trap: pointing to A because there's no Imagine.
Fix: ask what is the first sentence doing? Student sees the question hook.
notes.prep: Decision point before drafting. Under 80% means the class writes a preview for this one together first.

slides.title: Preview it in one line
slides.pivot: cut each reason to two or three words, then join with commas
slides.followUp: cold call one board: which reason did you put last, and why?

items.text: Every class should have a pet. Reasons: responsibility, calm, science.
items.answer: Pets teach responsibility, calm us down and bring science to life.
items.expect: three short reasons in one sentence

items.text: Lunch should be longer. Reasons: time to play, time to eat, better focus.
items.answer: A longer lunch means time to play, time to eat and sharper afternoons.

items.text: Kids should help write school rules. Reasons: fairness, ownership, new ideas.
items.answer: Rules made together are fairer, kids follow them and fresh ideas get heard.

items.text: Our playground needs more shade. Reasons: sun safety, cooler play, comfy lunches.
items.answer: Shade keeps us sun safe, keeps play cool and makes lunch comfortable.

say: Each one has a position and three reasons.
Squeeze the reasons into one preview sentence.
trap: Fix: student cuts each reason to a few words, joins with commas and and.
notes.stretch: Put the strongest reason last and say why.
notes.help: Use the frame: ___, ___ and, most importantly, ___.
notes.prep: Guided practice on the part most often left out. SC2.

slides.title: Draft your introduction
slides.task: Work through your Worksheet, plan your four parts, then draft your introduction in your writing book.
slides.frame: I am writing to ask you to ___. ___, ___ and, most importantly, ___.

notes.answer: a four-part introduction aimed at one reader
beats: POINT to the task.
SAY: Planner open beside you. Every second line, so you can improve it later.
SAY: Read the task, complete each part, check your work.
Finished? Extension next. Everyone, together, on three.
CONFERENCE first with anyone from yesterday's exit list.
ASK: Swap with your partner. Show me how many parts you can find.
10 sec. Cue: Fingers at your chest... show me.
EXPECT: 4
TIME 20 minutes, including the swap at 15.
trap: a preview that lists more than three reasons.
Fix: student checks the planner and cuts to the three planned.
notes.stretch: Extension: make the parts flow, then write it for a second reader.
notes.help: Supported Worksheet: picture-clue choices, a starter for each part, a check.
notes.prep: Independent drafting. The introduction is the first paragraph of the published piece. SC2 and SC3.

slides.extendedTask: a worksheet ending in a plan, then the drafted introduction of the big piece

slides.title: Show what you know
questions: Every week, our class throws away bags of paper. Recycling bins would fix this. Our school must put one in every room.

notes.answer: e.g. Bins save paper, teach good habits and cost almost nothing
beats: SAY: A new introduction with a part missing. Add it.
ASK: Write the preview this introduction needs.
60 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: three short reasons in one line
RECORD who writes a single reason or a new position. Tomorrow's conference.
trap: Fix: none now, record the name.
notes.prep: Exit evidence for SC2 on a new introduction. One board per student.

slides.reflectionPrompt: Read your introduction to your partner. Can they tell you exactly what you want?

notes.answer: open - partner can name the position and the three reasons
beats: SAY: Let's read our I can lines together. Everyone, together, on three.
ASK: How sure are you that your introduction has all four parts?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up, sideways or down
RECORD each thumb down beside the exit boards.
ASK: Can your partner say exactly what you want?
30 sec. Turn and tell, partner B reads, partner A repeats the position.
EXPECT: You want the zoo to stop...
notes.prep: Self-assessment read beside the exit boards. SC2.
